Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: VisiBabble is described as an early speech intervention and clinical/research tool focused on reinforcing syllabic utterances associated with later language and cognitive development. The paper emphasizes prespeech intervention best practices, ABA experimental design, and measurement of syllables/utterances, indicating a primary utilitarian (therapeutic/assessment) goal. Fun/visual feedback (bird, frog, fireworks, faces) is added and iteratively adjusted to maintain engagement, but is clearly in service of the intervention aims rather than originating from an entertainment game or co-designed fun-first workshop. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design where the primary utilitarian mechanic is designed first and fun is incorporated to support it.

reasoning: The visiBabble system is described as using a responsive, child-initiated, child-focused 'play' mode of speech intervention without specific training events or explicit task structure. The child simply vocalizes and receives visual feedback; there is no mention of rules, goals, or game mechanics, which aligns best with unstructured play rather than any form of structured or rule-based game.

Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The study is not a multiplayer or competitive game; it is an ABA single-participant intervention where an infant produces vocalizations and a system provides visual feedback. There are no symmetric roles between agents; instead, the child and the visiBabble system have fundamentally different roles and capabilities (one vocalizes, the other analyzes and displays feedback). This maps best to an entirely asymmetrical interaction structure.
